fake_negative_hypotheses: The incorporation of cationic additives, specifically N,N-dimethylmethyleneiminium chloride at a concentration of 0.2M to 0.3M, and the newly identified methyl tetrahydrotriazinium ([MTTZ]+) at a concentration range of 0.1M to 0.25M, into perovskite precursor solutions will significantly enhance the stability and film quality of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs). This enhancement will be achieved through the in situ formation of [MTTZ]+, which improves the formation energy of iodine vacancies and increases the migration energy barriers for iodide and cesium ions during the film formation process. The optimized processing conditions will include a mixing temperature of 60°C and a spin-coating speed of 3000 RPM for 30 seconds. Comprehensive characterizations using photoluminescence spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM) will be employed to assess film quality and stability. Control tests involving traditional precursor formulations will provide clear benchmarks for efficiency and stability metrics, enabling a robust validation of the hypothesis through long-term degradation testing under specified conditions (e.g., 85°C, 85% relative humidity, and 1.0-sun illumination) over a period of six months.

The implementation of a hybrid computational modeling and machine learning framework that employs support vector regression and genetic algorithms will enable the prediction and optimization of concentration ratios of N,N-dimethylmethyleneiminium chloride and the methyl tetrahydrotriazinium ([MTTZ]+) cation in perovskite precursor solutions. By investigating specific degradation mechanisms including nonradiative recombination, thermal decomposition, and phase segregation, we will quantify stability and efficiency metrics under controlled environmental conditions of 85°C and 85% relative humidity. The methodology will incorporate an iterative feedback loop that cross-validates machine learning predictions with experimental validation to refine precursor formulations, ultimately enhancing the stability and efficiency of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs).

The integration of N,N-dimethylmethyleneiminium chloride and methyl tetrahydrotriazinium ([MTTZ]+) into perovskite precursor solutions at precisely optimized concentrations—identified through a hybrid machine learning framework that evaluates metrics such as power conversion efficiency, degradation rates, and cation reactivity—will significantly enhance the stability, efficiency, and reproducibility of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs). This enhancement is anticipated to occur through the in situ formation of [MTTZ]+, which modulates iodine vacancy formation energies and enhances migration energy barriers for iodide and cesium ions. Comprehensive validation will involve long-term stability testing under controlled laboratory conditions (85°C and 85% relative humidity) for a minimum of six months, as well as advanced characterization techniques including X-ray diffraction and atomic force microscopy to quantitatively assess improvements in film stability and quality.

The synergistic integration of a cationic additive system, specifically incorporating N,N-dimethylmethyleneiminium chloride (0.2M to 0.3M) and methyl tetrahydrotriazinium ([MTTZ]+, 0.1M to 0.25M), within a triphasic solvent system comprised of 40% toluene, 40% N-methylpyrrolidone, and 20% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), operated under an optimized vacuum flash methodology (depressurization rates between 50-200 mbar/min), will enhance the efficiency, stability, and reproducibility of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs). This enhancement will manifest through improved film crystallinity, grain size, and reduced iodine vacancy concentrations, thereby significantly mitigating nonradiative recombination processes. Validation of this hypothesis will involve comprehensive measurements using photoluminescence spectroscopy to quantify nonradiative losses, X-ray diffraction to analyze crystallinity and phase stability, and scanning electron microscopy to assess film morphology and defect density. Long-term degradation testing under challenging environmental conditions (85°C, 85% relative humidity, and 1.0-sun illumination) over six months will benchmark the performance of these optimized PSMs against traditional solar module formulations, providing clear evidence of their commercial viability.

The combination of a hybrid solvent system utilizing acetonitrile (ACN) at a concentration of 0.5-1.0 M with a 5% volume of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) alongside cationic additives N,N-dimethylmethyleneiminium chloride (0.2M to 0.3M) and methyl tetrahydrotriazinium ([MTTZ]+) (0.1M to 0.25M) will synergistically enhance the crystallinity, film morphology, and stability of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs). Specifically, this combination will: 1) reduce defect states and enhance migration energy barriers for iodide and cesium ions during film formation, and 2) promote a single crystallization pathway via a dimethyl sulfoxide-solvated intermediate phase to α-FAPbI3, minimizing heterogeneous nucleation. Comprehensive characterizations, including detailed parameters (scanning speed in SEM of 10 µm/s, XRD step size of 0.02° and AFM scan size of 5 µm) alongside long-term performance testing under varied environmental conditions (85°C, 75-85% relative humidity, and 1.0 sun illumination for six months), will validate the enhanced efficiency and stability of the optimized PSMs compared to control formulations.
gold_hypothesis: The synergistic combination of [Bcmim]Cl and MACl effectively stabilizes the perovskite precursor solution (PPS) by inhibiting the condensation reaction between MACl and formamidinium iodide (FAI), leading to the formation of phase-homogeneous and stable perovskite films with high crystallinity, fewer defects, and preferential crystal growth orientations, resulting in record-certified efficiencies and enhanced long-term operational stability for large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs).

Incorporating an optimal concentration of methylammonium chloride (MACl) (e.g., in the range of 30–50 mol%) as an additive in perovskite precursor solutions, under controlled environmental conditions (e.g., temperature and humidity optimized for film deposition), will improve the efficiency, long-term stability, and reproducibility of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs). This improvement is achieved by stabilizing intermediate phases during the film-formation process, enhancing grain size, phase crystallinity, and defect passivation, ultimately bridging the gap between laboratory-scale devices and commercially scalable solar products. The validity of this hypothesis will be assessed by systematically comparing large-area perovskite films fabricated with and without MACl, particularly through roll-to-roll deposition techniques for scalable manufacturing.

Incorporating a novel ionic liquid, engineered with dual-functional groups for enhanced hydrophobicity and crystallinity, into the perovskite precursor solution will enable the scalable fabrication of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs) by improving film quality and reducing precursor degradation. This process will focus on utilizing slot-die coating to achieve uniform 20% larger grain sizes over substrates exceeding 100 cm², minimizing defect density, and enhancing moisture resistance by 50% during solution storage. The hypothesis will be empirically tested using a combination of inline spectroscopic monitoring and large-area X-ray diffraction to ensure reproducibility and rapid implementation at an industrial scale.

Incorporating a dual-additive system comprising [Bcim][TFSI], a multifunctional ionic liquid, and a specifically tailored perovskite-compatible polymer such as PVDF-HFP (poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene)) can enhance the stability, scalability, and reproducibility of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs). The polymer serves both as a stabilizing matrix to maintain film integrity during crystallization and as a moisture barrier to reduce environmental degradation, while [Bcim][TFSI] promotes uniform crystallization and grain growth through its Lewis-basic CN groups and hydrophobic interactions. By optimizing low-temperature processing (e.g., below 150°C annealing with solvent incorporation techniques such as dimethyl sulfoxide), this approach addresses challenges in precursor degradation and incomplete crystallinity, while maintaining high optoelectronic performance. Validation will include metrics such as achieving a PCE >20% for modules >10 cm², film roughness below 5 nm RMS, and stability (retention >90% PCE after 1000 hours at 85°C/85% RH).

Incorporating a specifically engineered dual ionic liquid system, featuring [Bcim][TFSI] and a secondary ionic liquid such as 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium trifluoromethanesulfonate ([EMIm][OTf]), combined with a perovskite-compatible polymer matrix like PVDF-HFP tailored for low-temperature processing (e.g., 100–130°C in an inert atmosphere), will enhance the efficiency, stability, and scalability of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs). This optimized hybrid system will target the production of large-area PSMs that achieve ≥25% larger grain sizes and defect density reduction of 40% on >100 cm² substrates, maintain a power conversion efficiency (PCE) above 22%, and improve moisture resistance by at least 75%. Performance metrics will be validated through controlled spectroscopic methods, such as in situ Raman and UV-Vis spectroscopy, as well as real-time thermal stability tests over 1,500 hours under 85°C/85% RH conditions, demonstrating commercial viability and industrial-scale applicability.

Introducing a sequential deposition technique that initially applies a low concentration (10–20 mol%) of methylammonium chloride (MACl) during the precursor solution preparation stage, followed by a high-concentration MACl vapor treatment (40–60 mol%, vaporized at controlled conditions of 80–100 °C and 20–30 minutes exposure) post-deposition, can significantly enhance the efficiency, stability, and reproducibility of large-area perovskite solar modules. The two-step technique is hypothesized to support controlled nucleation during solution processing, optimize crystal growth during vapor treatment, and improve defect passivation at both the microscale (grain size, crystallinity) and macroscale (film uniformity across extended surfaces). Validation will include evaluating the stability of perovskite films over 1,000 hours under accelerated aging tests and achieving module efficiencies exceeding 20% for areas >100 cm².

Validation will include systematic characterization of phase transition dynamics, crystal quality, and degradation pathways under operational stress to ensure insights for industrial translation."

The synergistic application of multifunctional ionic liquids, specifically 1,3-bis(cyanomethyl)imidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide ([Bcim][TFSI]), in conjunction with optimized concentrations of methylammonium chloride (MACl) (1-3% by weight) and ammonium bromide (ABr) (1-5% by weight) in perovskite precursor solutions, will significantly enhance the efficiency (targeting >23% power conversion efficiency), long-term stability (maintaining >85% efficiency after 1,000 hours of accelerated testing), and reproducibility of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs). This enhancement will manifest through improved crystallization and grain growth, characterized by grain sizes > 1 μm, enhanced thermal stability indicated by a 25% increase in decomposition temperature compared to control films, and reduced degradation rates, with structural quality assessed via X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and current-voltage (I-V) characteristics. Rigorous control experiments will verify the statistical significance of these enhancements against traditional precursor formulations.

The incorporation of multifunctional ionic liquids, particularly 1,3-bis(cyanomethyl)imidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide ([Bcim][TFSI]) and similar compounds, into perovskite precursor solutions at concentrations ranging from 5% to 15% (by weight) will enhance the efficiency, stability, and reproducibility of large-area perovskite solar modules. This enhancement will be evidenced by increased grain size (≥ 1 μm), improved crystallinity as indicated by X-ray diffraction peaks, and superior thermal stability evidenced by a 20% higher decomposition temperature compared to control films without ionic liquids. Controlled experiments will compare these metrics against those of traditional precursor solutions, with statistical analysis verifying significance.

The addition of optimized concentrations of ammonium bromide (ABr) (1-5% by weight) as a co-additive with specific concentrations of methylammonium chloride (MACl) (0.5-2% by weight) in perovskite precursor solutions will enhance the efficiency (targeting >20% power conversion efficiency), stability (retaining >80% performance after 1000 hours of accelerated testing), and reproducibility of large-area perovskite solar modules (PSMs). This enhancement will be achieved by promoting improved crystallization processes, reducing degradation rates, and improving film quality, characterized through X-ray diffraction (XRD) for crystallization assessment, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for morphology evaluation, and current-voltage (I-V) curves for electrical performance metrics.
